identity.title: ALMA Survey of Orion Planck Galactic Cold Clumps (ALMASOP): A Hot Corino Survey toward Protostellar Cores in the Orion Cloud

paper_type_evidence.quote: Aiming to investigate the occurrence of COMs and their possible origins, we conducted a chemical census toward a sample of protostellar cores as part of the ALMA Survey of Orion Planck Galactic Cold Clumps (ALMASOP) project.

The observations toward the 72 targets of the ALMASOP project were carried out with both the 12-m array (in two configurations: C43–5 and C43–2 represented respectively by TM1 and TM2) and the 7–m array (ACA) of ALMA

analysis_steps.goal: Preliminary search for COMs and source selection

method.value: Extract spectra at the 1.3 mm continuum peak pixel for all 56 Class 0/I protostellar cores and select sources with at least two CH3OH transitions detected at SNR > 5 (including at least one with E_up > 100 K).

evidence.quote: To have a quick search of the presence of COMs, we first extract the spectra at the continuum peak pixel for the protostellar cores from the ALMASOP sample.

Among the 56 protostellar cores, we find 11 sources with at least two CH$_3$OH transitions including at least one transition with upper energy $E_\mathrm{up}$ $>100$ K getting detected at a level above 5$\sigma$.
We select the sources where at least two methanol transitions are detected (SNR $>$ 5)

key_parameters.value: At least one transition with E_up > 100 K

evidence.quote: including at least one transition with upper energy $E_\mathrm{up}$ $>100$ K getting detected at a level above 5$\sigma$.

analysis_steps.goal: Measure source emission size and H2 column density, and extract source-averaged spectra

method.value: Perform 2D Gaussian fitting on the CH3OH-46K (218440 MHz) moment-0 images in CASA to define the emission extent, extract full spectra within this extent, and compute H2 column density N(H2) from 1.3 mm continuum flux within the same extent.

evidence.quote: define their emission extent based on the 2D Gaussian fitting of their CH$_3$OH moment–0 images. The CH$_3$OH transition we use is at $J=4-3$; $K_a=2-1$; $K_c=3-2$; $E_\mathrm{up}$ $=46$ K; and $f_\mathrm{rest}$ $= 218440$ MHz (hereafter CH$_3$OH–46K transition)
We then extract the full spectra within the same extent toward each source.

Based on the 2D Gaussian fitting in CASA to the CH$_3$OH–46K transition moment–0 images, we infer the extent of the methanol emission and calculate the molecular hydrogen column density $N(\mathrm{H_2})$ using the 1.3 continuum flux within the extent.

key_parameters.value: Reference line: CH3OH J=4-3, Ka=2-1, Kc=3-2 at 218440 MHz (E_up = 46 K)

evidence.quote: The CH$_3$OH transition we use is at $J=4-3$; $K_a=2-1$; $K_c=3-2$; $E_\mathrm{up}$ $=46$ K; and $f_\mathrm{rest}$ $= 218440$ MHz (hereafter CH$_3$OH–46K transition)
We use the formulae in (cite: Hsu2020_ALMASOP) and (cite: 2008Kauffmann_CONTFormula) for optically thin continuum emission.

assumptions.value: Dust opacity law kappa_nu = 0.1 (nu / 1 THz)^beta cm^2 g^-1 with beta = 1.70

evidence.quote: The dust opacity is in the form of $\kappa_\nu = 0.1(\nu / 1\,\mathrm{THz})^\beta \mathrm{cm}^2 \mathrm{g}^{-1}$. The dust opacity index $\beta$ was assigned to be 1.70
We assumed a (dust) temperature of 100 K, which is the typical value for hot corinos.
Based on the 2D Gaussian fitting in CASA to the CH$_3$OH–46K transition moment–0 images

analysis_steps.goal: Identify molecular transitions and fit LTE synthetic spectra

method.value: Use XCLASS LineIdentification to identify molecular carriers and simulate 1D LTE synthetic spectra to fit T_ex, N, delta_v, and v_LSR for each species, first individually and then simultaneously for all species to account for line blending.

evidence.quote: we use XCLASS (cite: 2017Moller_XCLASS) to search for the molecular carrier candidates with its `LineIdentification` function, and to simulate synthetic spectra with input molecular parameters including the excitation temperature ($T_\mathrm{ex}$), total column density ($N$), line width in velocity ($\delta v$), and local-standard–of–rest velocity ($v_\mathrm{LSR}$).
We then run overall fittings for all species simultaneously with Bees algorithm and LM algorithm for each source to take into account blending of lines.

key_parameters.value: T_ex range limited to (0, 400) K for initial fitting

evidence.quote: To have a first estimation, we make individual fittings for each molecular species with the Bees algorithm, and the range of $T_\mathrm{ex}$ is limited to be (0, 400).

assumptions.value: Local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) for each gaseous molecular component

evidence.quote: Each (gaseous) molecular component is assumed to be in its individual local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE).

assumptions.value: Emission size of all species equals the deconvolved 2D Gaussian extent of the CH3OH-46K transition

evidence.quote: We assume the emission size of all species to be the (2D Gaussian) extent of the CH$_3$OH–46K transition deconvolved by the beam size.

assumptions.value: T_ex = 100 K fixed for molecules detected with only one transition

evidence.quote: For molecules detected with only one transition, we assume their $T_\mathrm{ex}$ to be 100 K, the typical temperature of a hot corino.

fitting.value: Bees swarm optimization and Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) algorithms in MAGIX, with uncertainties estimated via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) in XCLASS

evidence.quote: The optimization algorithms in MAGIX we use are “Bees algorithms” and “Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) algorithms”.

Tables 6 – 16 display the molecular parameters (i.e. $T_\mathrm{ex}$, $N$, $\delta v$, and $v_\mathrm{LSR}$) and their errors estimated by the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method in XCLASS of these 11 sources.

claims.hypothesis: COMs in hot corinos originate from thermal desorption of grain ice mantles in the warm (>100 K) inner envelope heated by the protostar.
claims.experiment: Measure deconvolved CH3OH-46K emission sizes and total gas-phase CH3OH molecule numbers (from 13CH3OH), model YSO SEDs with HO-CHUNK to infer >100 K warm region sizes, and test for correlations with bolometric luminosity L_bol.
claims.result: Deconvolved CH3OH extent correlates positively with the SED-modeled >100 K warm region size (ratio ~1), and both CH3OH extent and total CH3OH molecule number correlate positively with L_bol.
claims.finding: The positive correlations between luminosity, warm region size, and methanol extent/number support the thermal desorption paradigm for hot corinos.

evidence.quote: The luminosity of the hot corino sources exhibits positive correlations with the total number of methanol and the extent of its emissions. Such correlations are consistent with the thermal desorption picture for the presence of hot corino

The bolometric luminosity positively correlates with the extent and the total number of gas-phase methanol. Both of these correlations are consistent with the thermal desorption paradigm for hot corinos.

claims.hypothesis: The apparent difference in hot corino detection rates between the ACA-only data (8%), the combined 12m+ACA data (20%), and the Perseus PEACHES survey (56%) is driven by observational sensitivity, beam dilution, sample selection, and detection thresholds rather than intrinsic cloud differences.
claims.experiment: Compare beam filling factors and brightness temperature thresholds between ACA and combined data, and re-evaluate the Orion ALMASOP detection rate using the PEACHES sample selection (L_bol > 1 L_sun) and line detection threshold (3 sigma).
claims.result: Combining 12m and ACA data increases the beam filling factor by ~300x, raising the detection rate from 8% (4/48) to 20% (11/56). Applying PEACHES criteria yields 15/37 (41%) in Orion compared to 28/50 (56%) in Perseus.
claims.finding: Hot corino detection rates strongly reflect observational sensitivity and beam dilution; when matched in selection and SNR criteria, Orion and Perseus have statistically similar warm methanol detection rates given cloud distances and sample sizes.

evidence.quote: With the same sample selection method and detection criteria being applied, the detection rates of the warm methanol in the Orion cloud (15/37) and the Perseus cloud (28/50) are statistically similar when the cloud distances and the limited sample size are considered.

In contrast, the beam filling factor of this study is about 300 times higher than that of (cite: Hsu2020_ALMASOP), leading to much less beam dilution and much ease for the detection. The combined effect results in an increased detection rate of warm methanol from 8% in (cite: Hsu2020_ALMASOP) to 20% in this work.

claims.hypothesis: Hot corinos in the ALMASOP sample occur exclusively in Class 0 protostellar cores rather than Class I cores.
claims.experiment: Examine the multi-wavelength SED and near-IR slope of G208E, the only hot corino among the 11 classified as Class I by Dutta et al. (2020), and compare with Class 0 hot corinos.
claims.result: G208E lacks photometric data at 70-160 um where Class 0 SEDs peak, its fluxes at other wavelengths lie within the Class 0 hot corino range, and its near-IR (12-22 um) slope is steep like Class 0 sources.
claims.finding: G208E is likely a misclassified Class 0 core due to missing far-IR photometry, meaning all 11 detected hot corinos are likely Class 0.

evidence.loc: SED and Classification of Hot Corino
evidence.quote: The tentative steep slope at near–IR (12 and 22 $\mu$m) also makes G208E more similar to a Class 0 source. As a result, there may not be any Class I hot corino among the ALMASOP sample.
All the hot corinos we detect are therefore likely Class 0 protostellar cores.

claims.hypothesis: O-bearing COMs show uniform abundance ratios relative to methanol across different star-forming clouds if formed in the cold prestellar phase (e.g., HCOOCH3), whereas species sensitive to local environment (e.g., CH3CHO) show greater diversity.
claims.experiment: Derive column density ratios of HCOOCH3, CH3CHO, and C2H5OH relative to rescaled 13CH3OH (assuming 12C/13C = 50) and compare with hot corinos in other clouds.
claims.result: Rescaled ratios are 0.20% for CH3CHO, 1.9% for HCOOCH3, and 2.9% for C2H5OH; [HCOOCH3]/[CH3OH] is similar to literature values across clouds while [CH3CHO]/[CH3OH] differs.
claims.finding: The similarity of [HCOOCH3]/[CH3OH] and diversity of [CH3CHO]/[CH3OH] across clouds agree with the van Gelder et al. (2020) picture of prestellar vs. local-environment-dependent COM formation.

evidence.quote: The ratio of [HCOOCH$_3$]/[CH$_3$OH] appears to be similar while that of [CH$_3$CHO]/[CH$_3$OH] is different. This disparity agrees with what (cite: 2020vanGelder_COMs) suggested.

evidence.quote: Following the successful identifications of the hot corino sources with the ACA data in (cite: Hsu2020_ALMASOP), we further combined the ALMA and ACA data for gaining a better angular resolution.
In contrast, the beam filling factor of this study is about 300 times higher than that of (cite: Hsu2020_ALMASOP), leading to much less beam dilution and much ease for the detection.

why_this_method.value: Simultaneous multi-species LTE fitting in XCLASS/MAGIX accounts for line blending in line-rich spectra, and using 13CH3OH circumvents the high optical depth of main CH3OH.

evidence.quote: We then run overall fittings for all species simultaneously with Bees algorithm and LM algorithm for each source to take into account blending of lines.

Since there is no CH$_3$CN transition within our spectral coverage, and to circumvent the potential optical depth issue of CH$_3$OH, we consider the column densities of their $^{13}$C isotopologues, namely $^{13}$CH$_3$CN and $^{13}$CH$_3$OH.

referee_caveats_inferred: Assuming the same source size (the deconvolved CH3OH-46K moment-0 Gaussian FWHM) for all 36 molecular species in XCLASS ignores chemical stratification and excitation gradients across transitions.

Several species in Tables 6-16 hit or exceed the stated initial T_ex upper bound of 400 K (e.g., HCOOCH3 at 480 K in G192, 13CH3CN at 429 K in G211S), suggesting poorly constrained excitation temperatures or optical depth effects.
Using robust = 2.0 (natural weighting) maximizes point-source sensitivity but degrades angular resolution (~0.41-0.46 arcsec), leaving most COM emission regions only marginally resolved.
The chi-square values of the best-fit R06 SED models (Table 20) are very large (hundreds to >10,000), indicating poor formal fits or underestimated photometric uncertainties.
